### Section 2: Statement of Need

**[Rubric Tie-In: Clarity of Problem & Baseline Data]**
Low adult literacy and English language proficiency are critical, persistent barriers to economic mobility, health, and civic engagement in **[City/County Name]**. According to the **[Source, e.g., Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies / U.S. Census Bureau, Year]**, approximately **[X]%** of adults in **[County/Service Area]**—more than **[Number]** residents—score at or below Level 1 in literacy, meaning they struggle to read basic texts, fill out job applications, or understand prescription labels. This rate is significantly higher than the statewide average of **[Y]%** and the national average of **[Z]%**. Furthermore, this gap has widened since **[Year]**, driven by **[brief local factor, e.g., pandemic-related learning loss / shifts in the local economy / growing immigrant populations]**. Without targeted intervention, thousands of local families remain locked out of living-wage employment, which increasingly requires digital and functional literacy skills.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Target Population & Specific Barriers]**
The Community Literacy Project focuses its work on the residents most severely impacted by this crisis: low-income adults (ages 18+) residing in **[Specific Neighborhoods or ZIP Codes]**, where poverty rates reach **[X]%** **[Source, Year]**. Within these neighborhoods, our target population consists primarily of two overlapping groups: adults without a high school diploma or equivalency (**[X]%** of neighborhood residents) and English Language Learners (ELLs), who make up **[Y]%** of the local population **[Source, Year]**. These residents experience unemployment at **[X]** times the rate of the general county population and earn a median household income of just **$[Amount]**, compared to **$[Amount]** countywide **[Source, Year]**. For working parents in this group, the consequences are generational: research consistently shows that a parent’s literacy level is the single strongest predictor of a child’s academic success, contributing to the fact that **[X]%** of third-graders in **[Local School District]** currently read below grade level **[Source, Year]**.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Service Gaps & Urgency of Need]**
Despite the scale of this challenge, existing adult education infrastructure in **[City/County]** falls far short of demand. Currently, publicly funded adult education programs in our region have capacity to serve only **[X]%** of the estimated population in need **[Source/Local Coalition Report, Year]**. Remaining programs often require daytime attendance, charge fees, or are located outside of public transit corridors, making them inaccessible to low-wage shift workers and parents without childcare. At the Community Literacy Project, we see this unmet demand firsthand: over the past **[Number]** months, our waitlist for free evening and weekend literacy and ELL classes has grown by **[X]%**, with **[Number]** prospective learners currently waiting an average of **[Number]** weeks for a seat. 

**[Rubric Tie-In: Community Voice & Qualitative Data]**
Quantitative data only tells part of the story; our program design is directly informed by the lived experiences of local residents. In our **[Month, Year]** community needs assessment (n=**[Number]** residents and learners), **[X]%** of respondents identified reading, writing, or English proficiency as their single greatest barrier to securing a better job or supporting their children’s schooling. As **[First Name]**, a resident of **[Neighborhood]** and current waitlist member, shared during a recent focus group: 

> *"[Insert 1–2 sentence quote from a learner/resident about what low literacy prevents them from doing—e.g., 'I have worked at the same warehouse for six years. They want to promote me to supervisor, but I cannot pass the written safety test or write the shift emails. I just need someone to teach me after my shift ends.']"*

Without expanded, accessible literacy instruction through the Community Literacy Project, **[Number]** motivated adults like **[First Name]** will continue to face preventable barriers to economic stability and family well-being.

***

### 5-Item Checklist: Local Data Points to Pull
To finalize the brackets above, here are the exact five pieces of data you need to grab:

1. **County/City Adult Literacy & Education Rates:** Look up the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) PIAAC Skills Map for your county to get the exact % of adults at/below "Level 1" literacy, plus U.S. Census (American Community Survey Table S1501) for the % of adults without a high school diploma in your target ZIP codes.
2. **Target ZIP Code Demographics & Income:** From Census.gov (ACS 5-Year Estimates), pull the poverty rate, median household income, and % of residents who speak English "less than very well" for your specific service area vs. the county overall.
3. **Local School District 3rd-Grade Reading Scores:** Pull the most recent state Department of Education report card for your local school district to fill in the % of 3rd graders reading below grade level (helps prove the generational/community impact).
4. **Community Literacy Project Internal Waitlist Numbers:** Grab your internal intake numbers from the past 12 months—specifically the current number of people on your waitlist, the % growth over the last year, and the average wait time in weeks.
5. **Internal Survey Stat + Learner Quote:** Pull one clean percentage from a past learner intake form or survey (e.g., "% of students who enrolled to get a better job") and one real 1–2 sentence quote from an intake interview, survey comment, or student testimonial.

### Section 4: Program Design & Activities

**[Rubric Tie-In: Program Logic & Theory of Change]**
The Community Literacy Project’s program design directly addresses the barriers identified in Section 2—specifically low functional literacy, limited English proficiency, and inaccessible class schedules for working adults. Our theory of change is straightforward: if we provide low-income adults in **[Target Neighborhoods/ZIP Codes]** with free, flexible, contextualized literacy instruction paired with wraparound navigation support, then participants will achieve measurable literacy gains, secure higher-wage employment or promotions, and better support their children’s education *(see attached Logic Model, Attachment A, for full inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes)*.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Core Activities & Evidence Base]**
During the **[12-month]** grant period, we will serve **[Total Number]** adult learners across **[Number]** cohorts through three integrated, evidence-based activities:

1. **Contextualized Adult Basic Education (ABE) & English Language Acquisition (ELA) Classes:** We will offer small-group instruction focused on workplace and functional literacy (e.g., reading safety manuals, composing professional emails, navigating healthcare and school portals). Our curriculum is grounded in the Integrated Education and Training (IET) model, which research by **[Citation, e.g., U.S. Department of Education / OCTAE, Year]** demonstrates increases adult learner persistence and credential attainment by **[X]%** compared to traditional instruction. Classes will be held during evening and weekend hours at **[Location(s)]**, located within **[X]** blocks of public transit, with free on-site childcare and digital loaner devices provided to eliminate attendance barriers.
2. **High-Dosage 1:1 and Small-Group Tutoring:** Learners testing at the lowest literacy levels (NRS Levels 1–2) will be matched with trained volunteer tutors for supplemental instruction. Based on findings from **[Citation, e.g., ProLiteracy / National Research Council, Year]**, individualized phonetic and comprehension scaffolding accelerates reading gains for adult emergent readers by **[X]%**.
3. **Career & Family Literacy Navigation:** Each learner will work with a staff Navigator to translate literacy gains into real-world milestones, such as resume building, interview prep, passing workplace certification exams, or communicating with their children’s teachers in **[Local School District]**. Research from **[Citation, e.g., Center for Law and Social Policy, Year]** confirms that pairing adult basic education with case management increases program completion rates by **[X]%**.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Participant Pathway, Dosage & Timeline]**
Participants move through a structured four-stage pathway designed to maximize retention over each **[12-week / 16-week]** cohort cycle (running **[Number]** cycles per year in **[Months, e.g., Fall, Winter, Spring]**):

* **Phase 1: Outreach & Intake (Weeks 1–2):** Prospective learners are referred via **[Partner Organizations]** or pulled from our existing **[Number]**-person waitlist. Within **[X]** days of inquiry, staff conduct a 1:1 intake interview, complete a barriers assessment (childcare, transit, technology), and administer a standardized baseline reading/language assessment using **[Tool, e.g., CASAS / TABE / BEST Plus]**. Learners also co-create an Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) defining their personal career and family goals.
* **Phase 2: Core Instruction & Tutoring (Weeks 3–14):** Each cohort of **[Number, e.g., 15–20]** learners attends **[Number, e.g., two 2.5-hour]** group classes per week, plus **[Number, e.g., 1–2]** hours of weekly 1:1 tutoring and digital lab practice. By the end of the cycle, each participant receives a target dosage of **[Total Hours, e.g., 60–80]** instructional hours—meeting the state and federal threshold required to produce a measurable Educational Functioning Level (EFL) gain **[Citation, Year]**.
* **Phase 3: Post-Testing & Transition (Weeks 15–16):** Learners complete post-assessments on **[CASAS/TABE]** and update their ILPs. Those needing additional proficiency transition seamlessly into the next instructional level; graduates receive a completion certificate and transition into workforce placement or GED/high school equivalency pathways with **[Partner Name]**.
* **Phase 4: Follow-Up & Alumni Support (3 and 6 Months Post-Exit):** Staff conduct structured check-ins at 90 and 180 days post-exit to track job placements, wage increases, Promotions, and ongoing family literacy practices.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Staffing Structure & Oversight]**
Program delivery will be led by a qualified, culturally responsive team. The **[Program Director / Manager]** (**[X]** FTE, **[Qualifications, e.g., M.Ed. in Adult Education with X years experience]**) will oversee curriculum fidelity, partner referrals, and data compliance. Instruction will be delivered by **[Number]** Lead Instructors (**[X]** FTE total, certified in **[TESOL / Adult Education]**), supported by **[Number]** trained volunteer tutors coordinated by our **[Volunteer/Program Coordinator]** (**[X]** FTE). A bilingual **[Student Navigator]** (**[X]** FTE, fluent in **[Languages]**) will manage intake, barrier removal, and 90/180-day follow-ups. All staff and volunteers complete **[Number]** hours of pre-service training in trauma-informed adult pedagogy before each cohort launches.

**[Rubric Tie-In: SMART Outputs (Ready to cross-reference in Section 6)]**
To track implementation fidelity across the grant year, the Community Literacy Project will achieve the following measurable outputs:
* **Output 1 (Enrollment):** Enroll **[Target Number]** unduplicated low-income adults across **[Number]** cohorts by **[Month, Year]**, increasing annual program capacity by **[X]%** over our **[Year]** baseline of **[Baseline Number]** learners.
* **Output 2 (Instructional Dosage):** Deliver **[Target Hours]** total hours of group instruction and **[Target Hours]** hours of 1:1 tutoring, with at least **[X]%** of enrolled learners completing **[40/60+]** instructional hours (up from a baseline retention rate of **[Y]%**).
* **Output 3 (Navigation & Wraparound):** Complete Individualized Learning Plans (ILPs) and provide barrier-removal support (childcare, transit passes, or digital devices) for **100%** (**[Target Number]**) of enrolled learners, compared to **[Baseline Number/X%]** in **[Prior Year]**.
* **Output 4 (Tutor Mobilization):** Recruit, train, and match **[Target Number]** volunteer literacy tutors (a **[X]%** increase from our current baseline of **[Baseline Number]** active tutors) by **[Quarter/Month]**.

***

### Checklist: 4 Partner & Program Documents to Attach
To back up the claims in this section and score full points on feasibility, gather these four attachments:

1. **Logic Model (Attachment A):** A clean 1-page visual table showing Inputs → Activities → Outputs → Short-Term Outcomes → Long-Term Impact.
2. **Signed Partner MOUs / Referral Agreements:** 2–3 current Memoranda of Understanding with the organizations named in Phase 1 and Phase 3 (e.g., a local workforce development board, a Title I elementary school, or a community college for post-exit pathways) specifying how many referrals they will send/receive.
3. **Sample Contextualized Curriculum & ILP Template:** A 1–2 page excerpt of a workplace/functional literacy lesson plan Alongside a blank Individualized Learning Plan form to prove your program is structured and ready to launch.
4. **Standardized Assessment & Intake Packet:** A summary sheet showing the exact pre/post testing tool you use (e.g., CASAS or TABE) and your intake/barrier-assessment form.

### Section 6 & 7: Outcomes & Evaluation Plan

**[Rubric Tie-In: Measurable Outcomes & Baselines]**
Building on the implementation outputs established in Section 4, the Community Literacy Project tracks four SMART participant outcomes demonstrating measurable gains in literacy, economic mobility, and family engagement over the **[12-month]** grant period:
* **Outcome 1 (Literacy & Language Gains):** By program exit, **[X]%** (**[Number]**) of learners completing **[40/60+]** instructional hours will advance at least one Educational Functioning Level (EFL) in reading or English proficiency, up from our **[Year]** baseline of **[Y]%** (exceeding the state benchmark of **[Z]%**).
* **Outcome 2 (Workforce & Economic Mobility):** Within 180 days of exit, **[X]%** (**[Number]**) of job-seeking or underemployed learners will obtain employment, secure a wage increase/promotion, or enroll in postsecondary/credential training, up from a baseline of **[Y]%**.
* **Outcome 3 (Workplace & Functional Milestone Attainment):** By program exit, **[X]%** (**[Number]**) of learners will achieve at least two personal functional goals defined in their Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) (e.g., passing a written driver’s or safety exam, navigating a healthcare portal), up from a baseline of **[Y]%**.
* **Outcome 4 (Family Literacy Engagement):** By program exit, **[X]%** (**[Number]**) of participating parents/caregivers will report increased frequency of reading with their children or communicating with **[Local School District]** teachers, compared to **[Y]%** at intake baseline.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Evaluation Questions & Measurement Instruments]**
Our mixed-methods evaluation is structured around three core evaluation questions and validated tools:
1. *To what extent do participants achieve statistically significant literacy/ELA gains?* **Instrument:** Standardized NRS-approved pre/post assessments (**[CASAS / TABE / BEST Plus]**).
2. *How effectively do literacy gains translate into economic and family milestones?* **Instruments:** Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) rubrics, verified employment/wage records, and the **[Name of Survey, e.g., CLP Family & Career Mobility Survey]**.
3. *Which program components and wraparound supports most strongly predict learner retention?* **Instruments:** Attendance/dosage logs in **[Database Name, e.g., LACES / Salesforce]** and end-of-cohort learner feedback surveys.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Data Collection Schedule, Roles & Analysis]**
Data is collected across four structured intervals: **Intake (Week 1–2)** for baseline **[CASAS/TABE]** testing, demographics, and family literacy baselines; **Mid-Point (Week 8)** for formative ILP reviews and attendance audits; **Exit (Week 15–16)** for post-testing after **[40/60+]** hours of instruction and program satisfaction surveys; and **Follow-Up (90 and 180 Days Post-Exit)** for employment, wage, and educational transition verification. Certified Instructors administer assessments, while the **[Student Navigator]** tracks wraparound services and conducts post-exit follow-ups. The **[Program Director]**, supported by **[an external evaluator / our Data Manager]**, audits and analyzes data quarterly in **[Database Name]** to disaggregate outcomes by race, gender, and starting literacy level, driving continuous curriculum and schedule adjustments.

**[Rubric Tie-In: Data Privacy & Ethical Safeguards]**
All evaluation activities strictly adhere to federal and state privacy standards, including FERPA guidelines for adult learners. Because this evaluation constitutes routine program monitoring and quality improvement rather than generalizable human-subjects research, formal IRB review is not required **[or: is covered under an IRB exemption via Partner University]**. All learners sign multilingual informed-consent and data-release forms at intake. Personal Identifiable Information (PII) is stored in encrypted, role-restricted cloud databases (**[Database Name]**), and all data shared with funders or stakeholders is fully de-identified and reported only in aggregate.
